extracted_relationships.sentence: My grandparents on my father's side lived in Nitra when my father was young.
My grandfather was named Bernat Goldberger, and his wife was named Terezia Goldbergerova.
My grandfather died around 1935 to 1937, and my grandmother a few years before him.
They're both buried in the Jewish cemetery in Nitra.
My mother's parents were from Trstena, on the Orava River.
My grandfather was named Markus Lubovic.
Grandpa had a bakery in Trstena.
Then my parents found him an apartment in Vrutky, where he moved together with his second wife.
During the war they were both deported and died.
Lina married a barber in the town of Nowy Targ in Poland.
My father was named Heinrich Goldberger.
He was born on 17th July 1898 in Nitra.
He died in 1978, he was exactly 80.
Later he opened his own store in Zilina.
My mother was born in 1900 in Trstena.
She was deported and after that we didn't find out any more about her.
They worked for that Mendl, they had a relatively decent salary.
I also remember that as a young man he served as a soldier in World War I.
We lived in several places in Zilina, depending on how our financial situation was declining.
From there we moved to Vrutky.
We used to attend the big Neolog synagogue in Zilina.
My father even sent me to the yeshivah in Zilina.
My father's oldest brother was Jozef; he ran the store after Grandpa.
He and his family lived in Grandpa's house.
Tibor moved to Ecuador and Magda to Sweden.
Gyula lived in Nitra with his family.
He owned a radio store, where they also repaired radios.
They lived on Spitalska Street.
During the war they ended up in Terezin.
The entire family survived the Holocaust and after the war they ran away to what today is Israel.
Cecilia married Mr. Horn, who had a barbershop in Nitra on Hlavna [Main] Street.
They lived in an apartment above the shop.
Only one of my father's siblings, Rudi, survived World War II.
He then moved with his family to Palestine in 1946 or 1947.
The rest of my father's siblings died during the war.
My mother's oldest sister was named Lina.
She married a barber by the name of Löwenberg in the Polish town of Nowy Targ.
I know that they had two children that died along with Lina during the war.
Another of my mother's sisters, Ruzena, also died during the war.
Before the war she lived for some time with us in Zilina, and then also in Vrutky.
He died along with the others during the Holocaust.
I, Alexander Gajdos [born Goldberger], was born on 8th April 1924 in Zilina.
Then I transferred to the elementary Jewish school in Zilina.
The bar mitzvah itself took place in the synagogue in Vrutky.
Besides me, my parents also had my sister Viera.
She was born in Zilina in 1927.
Unfortunately, my sister didn't survive the war.
She went to the camp together with our mother, but we don't know at all where they disappeared.
During the war they interned our whole family in the collection camp in Zilina in 1942.
We used to go work on the construction of a sports stadium in Zilina.
My father also worked there.
My mother worked in the camp kitchen.
During the uprising my father, mother and sister hid in the forests around Rajecke Teplice.
They then caught them all there.
They took my father somewhere else than my mother and sister.
My father got into Sachsenhausen and then into Buchenwald.
My mother and sister were sent to the women's camp in Ravensbrück.
During the uprising I joined the army.
Before the war I'd been a member of the Hashomer Hatzair youth movement.
We were part of some defenses in Strecno.
They took me to the hospital in Martin.
They quickly evacuated us to the town of Sliac.
I set out for the partisan headquarters, and he said that he wouldn't go there.
From the hospital I went to Banska Bystrica, to the headquarters.
There they accepted me into the guard detachment.
I stood guard in front of the headquarters on the main square in Banska Bystrica.
People were being evacuated into the mountains, Stare Hory, Donovaly, Kozi Chrbat.
So they captured us.
Eventually they put us on a train and took us to a prison in Banska Bystrica.
We were there from the beginning of December until the end of February.
Once in some hubbub, they'd chase someone out to Kremnicka.
They would chase them out there with dogs, machine guns.
Then they'd round them up again, and go shoot them all again.
The ones that were here before you, they've all been killed in Kremnicka!
So they led us there, into a hallway.
Across the street was the Banska Bystrica courthouse, and that's where they had their headquarters.
Of course, they took us prisoner and led us off to some village.
The next day he sent us with a soldier back to Banska Bystrica.
We again set out in the same direction as the day before.
The second time around, we managed to get to the village of Priechod.
We told him that we'd like to join some partisan unit.
They told us that up above the village there was a gamekeeper's lodge with a partisan unit.
We moved ourselves over to the lodge.
In the morning, the village of Priechod had been surrounded by the Germans.
As people ran out the houses, the Germans shot them straight off, like rabbits.
They gathered up part of the men and led them off to the edge of the village under a steep hill.
As they were running, they shot them all.
Finally the Germans torched the village.
In the end the Russians caught and executed him.
From there we used to go on patrols to the surrounding villages.
We gradually moved from the gamekeeper's lodge to bunkers in the forest.
At the end of February, beginning of March we continued through Chabenec and the Low Tatras to Brezno.
Brezno had already been liberated.
There were Romanian soldiers there.
Czechs and Slovaks marched in the direction of Poprad.
After arriving in Poprad I reported to the First Czechoslovak Army Corps.
There I was accepted into junior officers' school.
I graduated from junior officers' school in the army corps with the rank of lance corporal.
Since then I've worked my way up to lieutenant colonel in the Czechoslovak Army.
After finishing school I left with the other soldiers, as part of our training, on foot from Poprad to Martin.
In Martin we met President Benes, who'd come from Kosice.
There we boarded some vehicles and they sent us as reserves to Moravia.
In this way we followed the front all the way to Prague.
In Prague, we as soldiers used to go on 'maneuvers.'
At the end of June they sent us back to Slovakia, to the army column in Nitra.
While I was in Nitra I stayed with my father's brother, Rudi.
He survived the war in Terezin.
After several days I set out on a freight wagon from Nitra to Zilina.
In Zilina I met up with my father, who already had his own place rented.
To make ends meet, I began working as a plumber.
My father moved to Karlovy Vary still in the year 1945.
I joined them at the beginning of the spring of 1946.
I lived with my father.
My father got a job in a spa.
First he was in the oxygen shop, where they filled oxygen tanks.
Then he became an accommodation officer at the head office.
He stayed there until retirement.
During that time I met my first, today already deceased wife.
Her maiden name was Irena Rothova.
She was born in 1926 in the town of Kajdanove in Subcarpathian Ruthenia.
Kajdanove belonged to the Mukacevo district.
After the war she returned to Subcarpathian Ruthenia.
One of her mother's brothers lived in Karlovy Vary.
As luck would have it, it was Mr. Kleinman that my future wife came to stay with.
I met her at my father's friend's, Mrs. Katzova's.
We had a Jewish wedding, under the chuppah, in Karlovy Vary, in 1946.
We had a civil wedding in the fall of 1948.
We celebrated our wedding, the Jewish one, at the Kleinmans'.
My wife survived the war in Auschwitz.
From there she got to some factory and finally ended up in Terezin.
Her parents died in Auschwitz.
Besides her parents, she also had two brothers.
Both survived the war, and moved away, to Israel.
They were named Imre Roth and Bela Roth.
I later met Imre in Karlovy Vary.
My wife met up with him someplace in Budapest.
My wife died I lost contact with them.
After World War II, the activity of the Jewish community in Karlovy Vary was renewed as well.
The left mainly for Israel and America.
There was of course also a prayer hall here.
The community also had a rabbi and a shammash.
But the rabbi emigrated.
A couple of times a year, my wife and I would go to the prayer hall.
During totalitarian times, she was there to visit her brothers.
The first time was in 1965, I think.
Her younger brother, Bela, who lived in Beer Sheva.
Her older brother, Imre, lived in Natanya.
He had a furniture store.
Irenka worked as a seamstress.
After I arrived in Karlovy Vary, I worked as a caretaker for the company Czechoslovak Hotels.
I used to go around hotels fixing taps and similar things.
Well, and then I got the position of district secretary for culture for the KSC.
I was a member of the Party since 1945.
In 1970 they kicked me out of the Party.
Later I got a job as a construction technician.
I drove around to construction sites in the area.
In Karlovy Vary we initially lived in a small, cold and damp ground-floor apartment.
Eventually our two sons were born.
Milan in 1953, and Roman in 1956.
In time we also got a new, beautiful and sunny apartment on Vitezna Street.
We also used to go on vacations together.
We used to go as a family to Bulgaria.
My wife and I also used to go with the children on various camping trips.
Irenka also used to visit spas.
Mainly Frantiskove Lazne and around Pisek.
After the war, my father also got married.
He married a woman by the name of Eda Kleinova.
She was from Subcarpathian Ruthenia.
The four of them decided to buy a house in Prague together.
My father and his wife lived upstairs.
We of course used to visit them, about two or three times a year.
My father died in Prague in 1978.
His second wife died as well, about ten years after my father's death.
Irenka had a stroke at the beginning of the 1990s.
She died of it in 1994.
We buried her at the Jewish cemetery in Karlovy Vary.
In the meantime, our sons grew up.
Milan lives in the town of Tachov.
He's an electrician by trade.
But initially he worked in Tachov feeding cattle.
Roman graduated from civil engineering in Prague.
After finishing his studies he stayed in Karlovy Vary.
His office is right next door to the Jewish community.
He designs buildings, and is doing quite well.
Milan married a non-Jewish girl.
About five years ago, I went to visit Israel.
It was with a tour group.
I happened to be in Natanya during Sabbath.
At the turn of the millennium I met my second wife, Miluska.
She was working in the grocery store where I used to go shopping.
It ended up with us getting married.
Miluska isn't Jewish.
We had a civil wedding.
Miluska has three sons and seven grandchildren from her first marriage.
For several years I was on the board of the Jewish community in Karlovy Vary.
At one time I was vice president.
The president of the community at that time didn't meet the expectations of the rest of the members.
Finally, at one annual meeting Mr. Gubic spoke up.
Finally they voted that the former president would stay as the community's spiritual leader.
They elected me president.
This was about seven years ago.
My role is to take care of the community's property.
Religious matters are taken care of by Rabbi Koci and the shammash, Rubin.
As time passes, the community has less and less active members.
There are about ten of them.
There are seven of us on the board.
There are about 98 members in total.
Not all of them are right in Karlovy Vary.
We also have members in surrounding towns, like for example Sokolov and Jachymov.
The Jewish community has its own prayer hall.
Where people meet every Friday and Saturday to pray.
But Karlovy Vary is a spa town, with many guests, Jewish ones, too.
So it's nothing exceptional for even twenty men to gather here.
Some of the spa guests that have already been here several times automatically also come to the prayer hall.
We also observe the high holidays.
For Sukkot we also put up a sukkah in the courtyard of the community building.
